story.headline: Houthi attacks kill dozens of Yemeni troops
story.summary: Houthi missile and drone strikes on camps in Marib and Hadramout killed at least 30 government soldiers on 6 August, the deadliest escalation since the 2022 truce.
story.display_body: Houthi missile-and-drone assaults on Yemeni government camps killed at least 30 soldiers on Thursday 6 August 2026, the deadliest escalation since the 2022 truce. The Iran-backed Houthi movement struck military camps in the provinces of Marib and Hadramout, wounding around 50 more, according to Yemeni government officials; pro-government military sources put the toll higher, at 45 or above, and the Houthi spokesman claimed 'hundreds' of casualties — a figure that could not be independently verified. A de facto ceasefire between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government has largely frozen the fighting since April 2022 without any formal peace deal; officials called these coordinated strikes the most serious breach in years.
story.why: A collapse of the truce would reopen a war that had faded from view and risks drawing the Saudi-led coalition — and, indirectly, the broader Iran-US confrontation — back into open conflict.

story.headline: Netanyahu reworks Gaza disarmament deal
story.summary: Israel has rewritten the Board of Peace roadmap and Netanyahu said on 5 August that Israel will not withdraw before Hamas fully disarms, reversing the deal's core sequencing.
story.display_body: Israel has rewritten the Gaza disarmament roadmap it signed onto days earlier, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on 5 August 2026 that Israel had 'not agreed' to withdraw before Hamas is 'completely disarmed'. Under the Board of Peace framework that US President Donald Trump announced on 30 July — the multinational body (Egypt, Qatar, Turkey and the US) overseeing the ceasefire — Hamas was to surrender its weapons in stages while Israeli forces pulled back to the agreed 'Yellow Line'; Hamas accepted that version. Le Temps reports that Israeli-imposed modifications have since decoupled Hamas's disarmament from a full Israeli withdrawal, a change Hamas says voids its participation unless Israel meets its own obligations first. The characterisation of the reworked terms is contested — Israel presents them as clarifications, mediators and Hamas as a reversal of what was agreed.
story.why: A just-announced deal is being renegotiated before implementation, leaving the ceasefire's next phase in doubt.

story.headline: Teen gunman kills five at Thai school
story.summary: A teenage student killed five people at a school near Bangkok on 7 August after fatally shooting his grandparents, before he was also killed.
story.display_body: A teenage gunman killed five people at a school on the outskirts of Bangkok on Friday 7 August 2026 after fatally shooting his grandparents at home. Police said the suspect — a student enrolled at Debsirin Nonthaburi School in Nonthaburi province — opened fire with his grandfather's handgun, firing at least 26 rounds and carrying 34 more; at least 23 people were wounded, several critically. The attacker was also killed. Authorities initially reported six dead before revising the toll to five.
story.why: Mass shootings remain rare in Thailand relative to firearm-related violence overall, and a school attack by a minor will renew scrutiny of gun access in a country with high civilian ownership.

story.headline: Meta ordered to pay $567m in New Mexico
story.summary: A New Mexico judge ruled Meta a public nuisance and ordered it to pay $567 million over harms to children, on top of $375 million in March penalties.
story.display_body: A New Mexico judge ruled Meta a 'public nuisance' and ordered it to pay $567 million over harms its apps cause to children, in a decision issued late Thursday 6 August 2026. Judge Bryan Biedscheid in Santa Fe sided with the state, directing that $420 million of the sum fund treatment services for young people and the rest go to prevention and screening over five years; the award is on top of $375 million in civil penalties a jury imposed in March. The ruling also orders Meta to block New Mexico teens' access to its apps during school hours and overnight, set their accounts to private by default, and bar minors from 'romantic or sexualised' exchanges with its AI chatbots. Meta said it disagrees and will appeal.
story.why: It is one of the largest state-level penalties yet tying a social-media platform's design to child-safety harms, and its behavioural mandates could become a template other states copy.

story.headline: Turkey sends PKK disarmament law to parliament
story.summary: Turkey submitted a framework law on 5 August setting the legal basis to disarm the PKK, a key step in the peace process, with founder Ocalan reportedly signed off.
story.display_body: Turkey submitted a long-awaited framework law to parliament on Wednesday 5 August 2026 setting the legal basis to disarm the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK). The bill governs how PKK fighters lay down arms and the judicial handling of people linked to the group, and its imprisoned founder Abdullah Ocalan has reportedly signed off on the current draft. The government hopes to pass it before parliament's summer recess. Disputes remain: the PKK wants legal reforms on prosecutions and Kurdish political participation to accompany disarmament, while Ankara insists the group disarm fully first.
story.why: It is the most concrete legislative step yet in a peace process that could end one of the region's longest insurgencies, running since 1984.

story.headline: Dittli fights back with legal opinion
story.summary: Vaud state councillor Valerie Dittli released a legal opinion on 7 August finding her right to be heard was gravely violated in the Meylan report probe.
story.display_body: Vaud state councillor Valerie Dittli went on the offensive on Friday 7 August 2026, releasing a legal opinion that finds her right to be heard was 'gravely violated' during the cantonal government's handling of the Meylan report. The report, published on 24 April 2026, alleged that Dittli had secured a mandate and paid 10,000 francs of public money to the former head of a commission on agricultural land, who in return dropped a criminal complaint; a prosecutor opened a criminal investigation on the basis of it. Two constitutional-law experts commissioned by Dittli concluded the administrative-procedure guarantees were breached — deadlines too short, insufficient opportunity to respond — and Dittli, in a personal statement, called what she experienced 'extremely serious.'
story.why: The dispute over process, not just the underlying allegations, now shadows the Vaud executive and could bear on the criminal case against a sitting cantonal minister.

story.headline: US withholds F-35 audit report
story.summary: The Pentagon barred publication of a GAO report on F-35 production problems, the jet Switzerland has on order, RTS reported.
story.display_body: The US Pentagon has barred publication of a Government Accountability Office (GAO) report on F-35 production — the fighter jet Switzerland has on order — Swiss and French-language public broadcasters reported on 7 August 2026. A source told RTS the block, the first ever on a GAO report about the F-35, traces to the Pentagon; the GAO is the US federal audit office, roughly the counterpart to Switzerland's Federal Audit Office. Aviation analyst Bill Sweetman, a former Northrop Grumman manager, told RTS the report would likely show that numerous F-35 production milestones have slipped, evidence of 'very serious' programme difficulties.
story.why: Switzerland's roughly 6-billion-franc F-35 purchase has already drawn political fire over cost and delivery timing, and withheld data on schedule slippage feeds directly into that domestic debate.

story.headline: Vincenz appeal trial opens Monday
story.summary: The appeal trial of former Raiffeisen chief Pierin Vincenz opens Monday 10 August before Zurich's high court on fraud, corruption and mismanagement charges.
story.display_body: The appeal trial of former Raiffeisen chief Pierin Vincenz opens Monday 10 August 2026 before Zurich's high court, on charges of alleged fraud, corruption and criminal mismanagement. Vincenz, who ran Switzerland's third-largest banking group for years, was convicted at first instance in 2022; the appeal has been repeatedly delayed. Le Temps notes the case remains one of the highest-profile white-collar prosecutions in recent Swiss history.
story.why: The outcome will test how Swiss courts treat expense-account and self-dealing conduct at the top of a systemically important bank.
